body.p: utilizing opportunities for acquiring knowledge and understanding, for making himself understood; occasions for decision and action; opportunities for love and struggle; possibilities of work, of creative activity; occasions for worship; and every opening for liberty which provides any hope of possible existence.

And thus we perceive that philosophy cannot be satisfied with itself alone. On the contrary, it demands as inescapable for its own genuineness that the philosophical individual prove his worth by search and understanding in the realm of knowledge, by active participation and assumption of responsibility in public life, by reliability in his attachments to the human beings closest to him, by seeking existential understanding between himself and the adherents of an exclusive religious faith.

It is therefore by no means sufficient to renounce any kind of dogmatism and merely worship the wisdom of the eternally closed Hand of God which conceals the truth from us. No. Through our acts we must answer that Being which in its withdrawal somehow speaks to us, and, replacing unattainable knowledge, become conscious in our freedom of the reality of that derivative finite Being with which we have been endowed.

As Jaspers conceives it, philosophy is thus not a science. And if science should claim either to be able to solve the problems of philosophy, or authoritatively to reject it as being of no importance, it would be untrue to its own strict principles. Nevertheless, Jaspers himself looks on the pursuit of science not only as a necessary activity in itself, but also as one of the indispensable conditions for existence and for genuine philosophical thought. On the negative side it is science itself that, under the strict conditions of its general validity, allows the relativity and limitations of the scope of its findings to be clearly perceptible. On the positive side, philosophy finds in science the language — which changes in every era — which it needs in order to speak indirectly of transcendent Being. But there is more to it than this: by means of its general and empirical validity science, so to speak, maintains a standard of compelling insight which pursues existence even into those regions where it cannot be reached, where — instead — the uniqueness of existential obligation is realized. The absolutism of this obligation should itself be as clear as possible, and here again compulsive scientific insight acts as an unattainable but indispensable ideal which never ceases to demand complete clarity.
